claims.text: Depositing an ultrathin, high-temperature-stable lubricious oxide or silicate coating on an RHEA improves wide-temperature self-lubrication without sacrificing mechanical strength.
RHEAs incorporating refractory elements such as Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr can exhibit excellent high-temperature mechanical performance.
The proposed uncoated RHEA lacks inherent self-lubricating behavior.
An ultrathin oxide or silicate coating can form and maintain an in situ protective, low-friction layer on the RHEA.
The proposed material is intended for mechanical loading from room temperature to approximately 900 °C.
The coating forms a stable and continuous lubricious surface layer.
The surface layer minimizes frictional contact during mechanical interaction.
The coating leaves the bulk RHEA microstructure intact.
The coating provides a low-shear surface layer that remains stable at high temperatures.
The low-shear coating interface mitigates friction and wear.
Transferring friction-reduction functionality to the coating enables the RHEA to maintain its superior mechanical properties.
The coated RHEA will have a significantly lower friction coefficient than uncoated RHEA across the tested temperature range.
The coated RHEA will have a reduced wear rate relative to uncoated RHEA across the tested temperature range.
The coated RHEA will retain high strength during wide-temperature tribological service.
The coated RHEA will retain or improve oxidation resistance.
Uncoated RHEA substrates suffer from high friction under the proposed operating conditions.
Conventional MoS2-based self-lubricating materials undergo rapid lubricant degradation at elevated temperatures.
Conventional graphite-based self-lubricating materials involve a trade-off between lubrication and mechanical robustness.
Robust coating adhesion and integrity during repeated thermal and mechanical cycling are required for the proposed performance.
Coating delamination or disrupted layer formation at temperature extremes will cause loss of lubricious performance.
